card.name: Margamkali
card.tagline: Kerala's ancient Christian circle dance retelling Saint Thomas's mission.
card.profile: Margamkali is an ancient Indian round dance of the Saint Thomas Christian community, primarily preserved and propagated by the Knanaya sub-ethnic group in Kerala. Dancers wear traditional Chattayum Mundum attire and circle a central Nilavilakku lamp, which symbolizes Christ, while clapping and moving in a 14-stanza narrative cycle. The dance retells the life, miracles, and martyrdom of Saint Thomas the Apostle based on the 3rd-century Acts of Thomas. Traditionally performed without melodic instrumental accompaniment, the rhythm is kept solely by a singer playing a pair of small, palm-sized cymbals.
card.insight: Written in 14 stanzas free of Sanskrit in the 17th century, Margamkali is executed around a lit Nilavilakku lamp representing Christ, using no musical instruments other than a single pair of palm-sized cymbals.
card.profile_long:
Origins and History:
Margamkali is a traditional round dance belonging to the Saint Thomas Christian community of Kerala, India. Scholars have proposed multiple historical roots for the form, tracing aspects to Jewish wedding dances of the Malabar diaspora as well as native Kerala Brahmin traditions such as Sangam Kali and Yathra Kali. The word 'Margam' translates to path or way, historically referring to conversion to Christianity as 'Margam Koodal'. The core lyrical text documents the arrival of St. Thomas the Apostle on the Malabar Coast, his missionary deeds, the persecution he suffered, and the establishment of local churches. Historically, two distinct variants existed: a Northist (Saint Thomas Christian) version and a Southist (Knanaya) version. The extant 14-stanza structure was codified in the 17th century by the Knanaya priest Anjilimootil Itti Thomman Kathanar. The lyrics feature a language blend of Middle Tamil (Chentamil) and Syriac liturgical terms (such as Maran, Alaha, and Mishiha) without Sanskrit borrowings. Following suppression during the Synod of Diamper and periods of dormancy, the art form was revived around the turn of the 20th century by masters like Kalarikal Unni ashan and compiled in print by Puttanpurikkal Uthuppu Lukose in 1910. Research led by Dr. Chummar Choondal in the 1960s showed that active practice had become concentrated almost exclusively within the Knanaya community. Systematic institutionalization followed in 1995 with the founding of the Hadusa institute under Bishop Mar Kuriakose Kunnasserry.

How It Is Danced:
Margamkali is performed in a circular formation around a lit brass oil lamp called the Nilavilakku. A dozen dancers execute rhythmic step patterns, hand claps, and body bends that coordinate with the vocal narration. The performance is divided into two main sections (padham): the initial narrative section detailing the life of St. Thomas, followed by a dramatic martial segment known as Parichamuttukali featuring artificial swords and shields. A beginner starts by mastering basic synchronized side-stepping, heel taps, and measured hand-clapping patterns while maintaining spacing in the circle around the central flame.

Music and Instruments:
Unlike many classical Indian dance forms, Margamkali uses no melodic or heavy percussion instruments. The sole accompaniment consists of vocal chanting by a lead singer who plays a single pair of small, palm-sized cymbals to set the tempo and meter. The lyrics integrate Syriac devotional terminology alongside archaic Middle Tamil vocabulary, following traditional Cindu song structure.

Costume and Setting:
Performers traditionally dress in the classic Kerala white attire known as Chattayum Mundum. The setting is anchored around a central Nilavilakku (traditional oil lamp), where the standing flame symbolizes Christ and the circle of surrounding dancers represents the twelve apostles. While historically performed exclusively by men and young boys, contemporary performances feature female dancers in cultural venues and school youth festivals.

Occasions and Meaning:
Margamkali is performed on solemn Christian observances, community gatherings, weddings, and cultural festivals. The ritualized spatial setup serves as an act of living hagiography, bringing to life the apocryphal 3rd-century Acts of Thomas through physical devotion and oral storytelling.

Notable Figures:
Key historical figures include the 17th-century priest Anjilimootil Itti Thomman Kathanar, who edited the 14-stanza text; masters Kalarikal Unni ashan, Indumoottil Kocheppu ashan, and Indumoottil Kutto ashan; publisher Puttanpurikkal Uthuppu Lukose; 20th-century scholars Dr. Chummar Choondal, Fr. George Karukaparambil, and Jacob Vellian; and Bishop Mar Kuriakose Kunnasserry, who established the Hadusa institute.

Regional Variants:
While Northist and Southist variants existed in earlier centuries, only the Knanaya (Southist) tradition survived into the modern era, later codified and standardized for state youth competitions throughout Kerala.

Lineage:
Margamkali lineages were maintained through traditional master teachers known as ashans. The practice transitioned from village-based oral tradition to institutional preservation under Hadusa (All India Institute of Christian Performing Arts), which published the standardized text 'Margam kali Aattaprakaaram'.

card.sacred_note: Margamkali is a sacred Christian devotional art form centered on a lit lamp representing Christ. Outsiders should respect the sacred nature of the performance, lyrics, and symbolisms.

sections.origins_and_history: Margamkali is an ancient round dance of the Saint Thomas Christian community in Kerala, primarily maintained by the endogamous Knanaya (Southist) sub-ethnic group. Its origins are linked by scholars to Malabar Jewish diaspora dance patterns as well as Kerala Brahmin performance arts such as Sangam Kali and Yathra Kali. The word 'Margam' signifies the path to salvation, and historically 'Margam Koodal' referred to Christian conversion. The current 14-stanza composition was arranged in the 17th century by the Knanaya priest Anjilimootil Itti Thomman Kathanar, utilizing Middle Tamil (Chentamil) roots and Syriac liturgical terms like Alaha and Mishiha, devoid of Sanskrit vocabulary. After facing suppression under the Synod of Diamper and declining in practice, the dance was revived in the late 19th and early 20th centuries through ashans such as Kalarikal Unni and published texts by Puttanpurikkal Uthuppu Lukose in 1910. Sociological research by Dr. Chummar Choondal in the 1960s confirmed its preservation chiefly within the Knanaya community, leading to formal institutionalization at the Hadusa institute in Kottayam in 1995.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in a circular formation around a lit brass lamp (Nilavilakku). Typically executed by a dozen dancers, the performance consists of two main parts (padham): a narrative singing and clapping phase recounting Saint Thomas's life, followed by Parichamuttukali, a martial phase incorporating artificial swords and shields. Dancers synchronize rhythmic stepping and hand-clapping to the timekeeping of palm-sized cymbals played by the singer. A beginner learns by coordinating basic circular walking steps with rhythmic claps in unison around the central lamp.
sections.music_and_instruments: Margamkali features no musical instruments other than two small, palm-sized cymbals played by the main singer. The vocal text consists of 14 stanzas (padas) composed in a style related to Tamil Cindu literature, incorporating Syriac liturgical vocabulary such as maran (our Lord), alaha (God), mar thomma (St Thomas), malaka (angel), and Iso (Jesus).
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers traditionally wear the Chattayum Mundum, the traditional attire of Saint Thomas Christian women of Kerala. The setting centers on a lit Nilavilakku (oil lamp) placed on the floor; the flame represents Christ and the surrounding dancers represent his twelve disciples. Originally performed by men and boys, it is now widely danced by women and school students.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Margamkali is danced during Christian community celebrations, church feasts, weddings, and state cultural showcases. It serves as a visual and oral devotional recreation of the 3rd-century apocryphal Acts of Thomas, detailing his arrival on the Malabar Coast, his miracles, his trials, and the establishing of crosses and churches.
sections.notable_figures: Significant figures in the tradition include Anjilimootil Itti Thomman Kathanar (17th-century priest and lyricist), Kalarikal Unni ashan, Indumoottil Kocheppu ashan, Indumoottil Kutto ashan, compiler Puttanpurikkal Uthuppu Lukose (1910), Dr. Chummar Choondal (folk culture scholar), Fr. George Karukaparambil, Jacob Vellian, and Bishop Mar Kuriakose Kunnasserry.
sections.regional_variants: Historically, distinct Northist (Saint Thomas Christian) and Southist (Knanaya) versions existed. In modern practice, only the Southist (Knanaya) version remains in existence, codified today for standardized youth festival competitions across Kerala.
sections.lineage: The art form was preserved orally across generations through village masters called ashans. In 1995, the Knanaya Diocese of Kottayam established Hadusa (All India Institute of Christian Performing Arts), which published the authoritative text 'Margam kali Aattaprakaaram' to standardize and preserve the lineage.

claims.text: Margamkali is an ancient Indian round dance of the Saint Thomas Christian community in Kerala.
The dance is primarily propagated by the Knanaya sub-ethnic group.
The 14 stanza form was written in the 17th century by priest Anjilimootil Itti Thomman.
Margamkali uses no instruments other than two small palm-size cymbals played by the singer.

beats: Lighting of the Nilavilakku brass lamp at center floor.
Dancers step into the ring dressed in traditional white Chattayum Mundum.
The lead singer strikes palm-sized cymbals and begins the 14-stanza chant.
The circle moves in synchronized step and clap patterns.
Transition into the striking martial segment with artificial swords and shields.
